prefix.mes:
The road bent ahead of him, ruts baked hard by dry weeks, and Alderwatch grew as he walked: walls first, a grey line above the hedgerows, then the towers at the gate, then the noise — cart wheels, a donkey complaining, voices overlapping under the morning wind. The sword rode his hip the way it apparently always had, armor's weight settled on his shoulders like something worn a hundred times, and the walk told him this body was stronger than the one he remembered: no stitch in the side, no ache in the feet by the second mile.

The verge gave way to gravel, then to stone. Traffic thickened toward the gate — a carter with onions, two women with baskets, a boy leading a lame mule — and a short line formed before the arch, moving without much ceremony. A bored guard in a quilted jack looked each traveler over, waving most through with a nod.

The arch exhaled cool air as Alaric passed under it. The gate's shadow smelled of wet stone and manure, and beyond it the city opened up: a cobbled square just inside the walls, stalls with canvas roofs, a fountain crusted green at its rim, a steep lane climbing between plastered houses toward the higher town. Somewhere left, a smith's hammer kept a steady beat. A beggar sat against the wall with a wooden bowl, and a woman shouted down from a window about a delivery.

The morning went on around him, uninterested in who he was.

A porter came down sideways under a crate of turnips, and Alaric flattened against a drainpipe to let him by; laundry dripped somewhere overhead, and a shutter swung open and a woman tipped out a basin without looking first. At the left turn the blue sign creaked on its bracket, and beneath it the hall's door stood as promised — taller than any door had a right to be, oak strapped in iron, one leaf propped open to let out the noise of voices and a smell of tallow, leather, and old rain-soaked stone.

Inside, the ceiling went up two storeys. Morning light came slantwise through high windows and lay in bars across a flagstone floor scuffed dark by boots. To the right, a long counter with two clerks behind it, one stamping papers with a slow, dull rhythm; to the left, a board of notices thick with pinned slips, a couple of people reading it with their arms folded. Between them, rough wooden tables, some benches, a hearth still holding last night's ash. A party in mud-caked leathers sat arguing over a map at the far table, and a man in a mail shirt dozed upright against the wall, a spear leaning at his shoulder like a broom.

A few heads turned as the door let Alaric in — the habitual once-over that strangers got in places like this, nothing more — and went back to their business. The stamping clerk paused mid-blow, a slip of paper under her stamp, and looked over the counter at him.

prefix.mes:
The stamp came down on the paper she'd been holding, more to finish the motion than out of necessity, and she set the stamp aside.

"Registration." She said it like a diagnosis. She was a narrow woman with ink-stained fingers and hair pinned back with what looked like a sharpened quill, and she looked Alaric over the way a horse trader might — sword, armor, the state of his boots. "All right. It's two silver, one time, and that's you in the rolls for life. Every branch honors it — Crownheart, the coast towns, all of them."

She pulled a thick ledger across the counter and opened it to a fresh page, then dipped a pen.

"What the fee buys you: you take contracts off that board, we hold the client's coin so nobody cheats you, and the rolls travel between branches, so work done here counts everywhere. What it doesn't buy you: rank. That board on the wall posts what rank of work each contract wants — you're Novice the moment you sign, that's the standing, nothing personal. Your Power rank's a different animal entirely, that's what you actually are, and the measuring stone reads it. Some people like seeing the number." A shrug. "Some don't."

She turned the ledger toward him and held out the pen, its nib dripping a little.

"Name, and where you're from if you've got one worth writing. Two silver with the signature." Her other hand was already tapping the counter's worn spot, where a groove ran in the wood from years of coins being slid across the same place. Behind him the door boomed open and a gust of street noise came through with two mud-spattered men, and the second clerk called something to them that got a laugh.

The pen waited over the ledger.

The coins crossed the worn groove and her hand covered them without ceremony, one flick of the thumb to check the weight of each before they vanished into a drawer. The pen scratched through the ledger line — *Alaric Red* — and she turned the page back, scanned it, and nodded once, as much to herself as to him.

"Alaric Red. Novice." She said the rank like it was his first name. "Welcome to the rolls."

She reached beneath the counter and came up with a small tin plate, about the size of a spread hand, stamped with the Guild's crossed swords and a fresh-punched number along the rim. It had a plain leather cord through a hole in its edge. She set it on the counter between them, then laid her palm flat on it for a moment — and the tin warmed faintly under her hand, a shimmer crossing the metal like heat off a road.

"Bonded to you now. It knows your name and it knows your standing, and any branch desk can read it the same way. Don't lose it; replacing one costs more than joining did." She pushed it across with two fingers.

Then she nodded toward the far end of the counter, where a fist-sized crystal sat in a felt-lined cradle, dull grey until she touched it. It lit from within, a slow pulse of pale light, and settled.

"There's your number. Rank F, first stage — the stone doesn't lie and it doesn't flatter." She pulled her hand back and picked up her stamp again. "Guild rank and Power rank are different things, like I said. The board's that wall on the left, the desk's here, and work's wherever you find it. Anything else?"

The stamp hovered. The mud-spattered men had come up behind Alaric in the queue, one of them dripping on the flagstones, and the dozing man by the wall still hadn't moved.

She held the slip out. The paper was stiff, the seal embossed at the foot, blank where a second mark would go.

"That's your proof of work. When it's done, bring the slip back here and I'll mark it closed and count out your forty copper. Nobody at the tannery pays you — the client's coin's already in our strongbox, so Hessa Vell could be knee-deep in hides or gone to Crownheart by the time you finish, it makes no difference to your pay." She set the stamp down. "One adder, east bank of the tannery row, along the ponds path. Ten minutes' walk, out the east gate and follow the smell — you'll find it without directions."

Behind Alaric, one of the mud-spattered men was bargaining with the second clerk over the reed-flat serpents again, to judge by the rising tone.

"Anything happen out there that's not an adder — a second serpent, a man, anything with a knife — you come back and report it rather than being a hero over forty copper." She said it flatly, a line said a hundred times that week. "But it's one adder. Go kill it."

The path narrowed past the last shed, and the reeds closed in on the water side, tall as a man's shoulder, dry heads nodding. His boots pressed quiet into the packed mud. The adder lay on the bank.

It was longer than a man, thick through as his forearm, grey-green along the back with darker bands, and it lay in a loose coil with its head raised a hand-span off the mud, turned toward the warm water. Its eyes were lidless and gold. His boot sank past the ankle on the second step, and the mud sucked at it as he pulled free.

The adder uncoiled.

Not toward him — away, the long body pouring off the bank in one fluid run, loops sliding over loops, and the flat water took it without a splash worth the name. The gold eyes stayed on him the whole while, head riding a hand-span above the surface, and the wake it left was a thin V drawn straight across the shallow end toward the reeds on the far side.

By the time he had covered half the open mud the bank held nothing but the drag-line and the flattened grass where it had lain. The V-shrink of its wake reached the tall reeds past the warm runnels and slid in among them, and the stems shivered twice, then went still. The wake's line died somewhere in the green.

He stood on open mud with his sword still sheathed at his hip, the strike he had meant never made — the thing was long gone beyond any blade's reach, and the reed bed it had gone into stretched thick along the whole far shore. The warm water steamed on, indifferent. Somewhere behind him, back down the path, the tannery sheds clattered and sloshed on with their day.

prefix.mes:
He went along the water's edge, picking his footing where the ground ridged up firm between the runnels, sword still sheathed, eyes on the reeds and the shallows ahead. The mud told the story as he went: the drag-line fading, then a smooth wide groove in the silt under an inch of water where the body had crossed the shallows, then nothing but the ordinary stitches of bird feet and the pocked funnels of the warm springs.

The reed bed began where the bank ended, a wall of stems thick as his thumb growing out of standing water, leaning and whispering against each other. Where the wake had gone in, the stems were parted — a serpent-width channel pressed flat through the first few paces, the broken tops still pale and fresh. Beyond that the bed ran on along the shore, forty paces or more of it, dense all the way down to the waterline, and the water inside it black and still where the light didn't reach.

He stopped at the edge of the flat stems. No sound came from inside: no rustle of movement, no scales on dry leaf litter, nothing but the wind combing the tops. The channel through the reeds angled left and vanished into the dark of the bed, and whether the adder had kept going to the far shore, burrowed down into a tussock, or lay coiled three paces in among the stems was more than the eye could say from where he stood.

The water at his boots reached only to the shin. The reeds ahead stood close enough that a sword swing would meet stems before it met anything else.

The head came low and fast, and he was already bringing the sword around when the jaws closed on his shin just above the boot-top. Two points punched through cloth and skin, shallow, more a sting than a wound — the fangs found flesh and raked free as the serpent's weight carried it past his leg into the churned mud.

It was still coiling to strike again when his blade came down.

The longsword took it behind the head and went through, through scales and muscle, into the tussock beneath. The long body convulsed — a single violent whip that slapped water across his boots and flattened a fan of reeds — then whipped again, weaker, the tail thrashing the shallows out past the stems. He held the blade where it was until the thrashing thinned to a twitch, then to nothing, and the gold eyes fixed on nothing at all.

The bed went quiet around him. Somewhere out on the open water a bird called once and thought better of it.

His shin stung where the fangs had scored it, two thin lines beading red through torn cloth, and the black pond-water made them look worse than they were. The adder lay split in the ruined hollow of its own nest, longer up close than it had looked from the bank — longer than his arm and then some, scales the dull bronze of dead reeds.

The skin and a pair of the long hollow fangs were already in his pouch, gathered the way the pouch gathered things, without his hands ever touching the carcass. The System's tally of it all blinked at the edge of his sight and settled.

The reeds dripped. Out past the bed, the tannery sheds clattered on, and the contract slip in his pocket carried the Guild's seal, and the seal, he knew without looking, now read READY.

The water let him go reluctantly. He waded back out through the channel the adder had pressed, shin stinging with each step, and stood a moment on the firm bank wringing his boot-tops while the tannery row clattered behind him — scraping knives on hide, the hiss of the lime pits, a boy's voice shouting counts to somebody down the line.

The walk back into Alderwatch was half a mile of causeway between the ponds and the town's east gate. A carter with a load of oak bark for the pits overtook him at a walk and left him in his dust without a glance; a woman hanging washing paused to look at the torn cloth at his shin, decided it wasn't her business, and went back to her pegs. The gate guard waved him through on sight of the Guild plate at his belt.

The Guild hall sat where he'd left it, cool and dim after the bright shore, smelling of ink and old wood. A pair of hunters argued quietly over a map at the side table; nobody looked up.

The clerk behind the long counter was the same one, stamping something with a small practiced thump. He finished his line, then lifted his eyes.

"Back already." His gaze caught on the wet hems, the torn shin. "Marsh adder?"

The slip went onto the counter. The clerk picked it up, angled the seal to the lamp, and the READY caught the light back at him. He set the slip down, drew a ledger toward himself, and made one slow entry with a nib that scratched.

"Killed at the ponds, east bank path — that's the posting." He looked up once more, a brief assessing look at Alaric, at the reed-flats still clinging to his boots, then back down. "Alive when you went out. Alive when you came back. That counts."

He counted out copper from a drawer, forty of them, stacked in two flat rows, and pushed them across the counter with the slip.

"Cull's closed. Slip's yours to keep or bin." He was already reaching for the next paper in his tray. "Board's on the wall if you want more."

He pulled the slip from its pin and carried it back across the hall. The hunter's boots followed at an unhurried pace, stopping a polite few feet off.

The clerk read the slip, then looked up and held his eyes a moment longer than he had for the adder.

"Reed Flat Serpents. Ferry landings." He set the slip down flat. "You've seen the levels on it. Four to seven, and they run in company out there — the crossing men lost two dogs and nearly a swimmer to them this month. Solo work, that's your call." He dipped the nib. "Name's on your plate already. One stroke and it's yours."

The nib scratched. He drew a line of red wax along the slip's edge, pressed the Guild stamp into it, and the seal cooled from glossy to matte in the time it took to lift.

"Active." He slid the slip across, wax and all. "Kill count's five. Come back with the slip and it closes — no parts wanted, don't go hauling rotting serpent meat through my hall. Ferry landings are a day south on the Crown Road, then the river path. Crossing men know the Guild's work when they see the plate."

Behind him, the hunter shifted his weight.

"Ferry landings," the man said, to the clerk as much as to Alaric. His voice was flat, unhurried. "Shallows there run warm this time of year. Serpents sun on the flat stones past the reed line — you'll hear them slide in before you see them. Water kills your footing; they don't care." He unfolded his arms and shrugged once. "Or wait for company, if the Guild's paying you enough to share. Novice solo on that one's how the crossing men get their dogs back in pieces."

The clerk said nothing to that, only squared the slip on the counter and went back to his tray.

prefix.mes:
The Crown Road took him south out of Alderwatch between hedged fields, the afternoon sun warming his back. Traffic thinned as the town fell behind: a wool cart, two pilgrims walking with their hoods back, then long stretches of nothing but larks and the crunch of his own boots. His shin pulled at him with every stride, a dull reminder stitched into the rhythm of the walk.

Toward evening the land began to tilt toward the river. The hedges gave way to willow scrub, the air thickened with the smell of slow water and mud, and off to the west the Valedorn showed itself in glints between the trees, broad and brown-green and unhurried.

He reached the ferry landings as the light went long and gold. A wooden stage ran out over the shallows, pilings green with weed, a flat-bottomed ferry moored alongside. On the near bank sat a cluster of buildings — a toll house, a rope shed, a low tavern with a smoking chimney — and a handful of crossing men were beaching a skiff for the night, one of them wading in to the knee to haul its bow up the shingle.

They noticed him before he reached the stage. The talk among them dropped off. The one in the water straightened up, water sheeting off his arms, and looked him over — the plate at his belt, the sword, the torn shin.

"Guild?" the man called across the shingle. He didn't wait long for an answer; his eyes had already found the plate. "Then you'll be the serpent work." He waded out, wringing his sleeves. "Fair warning, then, and it's free. Two of my dogs gone this month. My brother's boy got bit to the hip and swam out by luck." He jerked his chin toward the reed line downstream, where flat stones lay bared by the low water, dark shapes stretched along them that might have been logs. "They sun out there at dusk. That's now."

Behind him, one of the other men had leaned his boat hook against the toll house and was watching, arms crossed, saying nothing.

prefix.mes:
The ferryman wiped his hands on his thighs and came a few steps closer, glad enough to talk.

"Safest footing's the shingle itself, this bank side. Coarse gravel, drains quick." He pointed downstream along the water's edge. "Stay off the mud where the reeds thicken — it takes your boots and holds them, and a held man's a dead man out here. The flat stones start about two hundred paces down, past the dead willow. You can walk the shingle right to them, dry all the way, but you'll be in the open while you do it. They'll see you long before you see the last of them." He scratched under his jaw. "Count's been five, six of a morning. Big one lies farthest out. The young ones take the near stones."

The other crossing man uncrossed his arms and spat, watching.

Alaric set off along the bank, and the ferryman called one last thing after him: "If you get one, drag it up the shingle. Others won't come far out of the water for a carcass, but they'll fight over one in the shallows."

The shingle crunched under his boots, the river sliding past on his left, brown and thick with evening. The dead willow came up on his right, silver branches bare, and past it the flat stones began — wide slabs of grey rock standing clear of the low water, still holding the day's heat. Four of the dark shapes lay along them, plain now as serpents: thick-bodied, scales the dull green of the reeds themselves, jaws resting open a finger's width. The nearest was the smallest, coiled at the edge of the group with its tail trailing into the water. Its head came up before he had closed half the distance, tongue flickering, the flat black eyes fixed on him. It did not slide in — not yet. It poured itself forward along the stone instead, a slow ribbon of muscle, gathering coils, and behind it the next serpent lifted its head too.

Twenty paces of open shingle lay between him and the near stone. The one facing him had stopped, neck drawn into an S, the whole front third of its body raised off the rock.

It poured off its stone in one long ripple, hit the water without a splash, and swam — head held high, a bow-wave curling off its snout, the reeds shivering along its path. The strike came, and he met it.

His sword swept across in a flat arc as the serpent's neck uncoiled, and the edge bit deep into the raised body just behind the head — a heavy, meaty impact, scales splitting, dark blood jumping. The serpent's mouth snapped shut a hand's width from his hip, its strike broken, and it collapsed sideways onto the gravel in a writhing tangle of coils, hissing like a kettle.

Then the second one hit him.

It came off the shallows where it had beached, jaws first, and its teeth caught him across the thigh before he could turn — a grinding clamp that tore through cloth and flesh, the backward-curved teeth hooking in and dragging. He heard himself grunt with it. Downstream, the other two serpents abandoned their stones entirely, sliding into the water and swimming hard for the bank, flat heads cutting toward the fight.

The wounded one struck at him from the ground, lunging on its ruined coils, and its teeth found the meat of his calf — shallow, tearing, a hot cramp of pain. The second serpent released his thigh and struck again, faster, catching the same leg lower, worrying the grip deeper before letting go.

Somewhere behind, back at the landings, a dog was barking — long, urgent barks carrying over the water, and a man's voice shouting something the wind took apart.

The serpent at his feet lay bleeding out on the gravel, still twitching, still snapping weakly at the air. Its larger kin stood between him and the river, head swaying, mouth open. The third one was hauling itself out of the water downstream, close now, water pouring off its neck. The fourth was still coming across the shallows behind it.

His thigh bled freely. His sword hand was steady.

The last serpent struck and he met it, point rising to take it through the open mouth. The steel went deep, punched out the back of its skull, and the whole heavy body slammed into him and the gravel together, jaws working on nothing, then nothing at all.

He shoved it off and sat there among the dead.

Four serpents on the shingle, all still, all leaking dark blood into the stones where the reeds grew. The river ran on. Downstream the dog barked once, far off, and quit. His own blood had soaked through his trouser leg and pooled under his knee, and his forearm was a ruin of torn meat, and his breath came thin and fast like a man who had run a long way.

Something stirred under all that hurt — not warmth exactly, more a settling, as if the fight had left something behind in his bones. It passed through him and was gone, and he couldn't have said what it was.

In his pouch, weightless, four skins and six fangs that hadn't been there an hour ago. The dead serpents lay where they fell, cooling, the evening coming down over the reeds in grey and gold.

He was alive. That was the whole of it for a while.

The cold was a slap. The forearm wound had crusted over with dried blood and road grime, and the first pass of water took the crust off and left the gash beneath open and raw, the skin around it puffy. He worked the water over it until it ran clear off his wrist, then braced a boot on the plinth and did the same for the knee, wetting the trouser leg and peeling it back. "Aye. Cord's on the nail." The smith was already back at the anvil, and the hammer took up its ring again before Alaric was out the door.

The way south ran through the edge of town and out along the ferry road, a rutted track between drainage ditches with the marsh opening out beyond them — grey reeds standing shoulder-high in every direction, stitched through with black channels of water. A heron got up somewhere ahead and beat away low over the reed tops. Two carts passed him heading in, one loaded with cut reed bundles, the driver giving him the flat once-over that strangers get and nothing more. The morning damp burned off slowly, and by the time the ferry landings showed themselves — two wooden fingers into a broad brown channel, a rope-ferry moored at the nearer one — the sun had found gaps in the cloud.

South of the landings the ground softened. He kept to the tussocks and the drier spine of a low bank, boots finding the ground the same way they had yesterday, and the reeds closed around him with their dry whisper. Water stood in the channels on either side, still as glass. Once something small plopped off a bank ahead and left rings, and once a snake-long shape slid from one channel into another far off to his left, too quick and too distant to be sure of.

He had killed three of the five here yesterday. The ground remembered it too: a churned stretch of mud near the bank, darkened with old blood, a torn reed bed where the last of them had thrashed.

He was still working south along the bank when the channel ahead of him broke surface — a slow V of ripple coming up the black water toward the bank he stood on, broad as a man's forearm at first, then wider. Ten paces on, the head rose out of the channel, water sheeting off a flat skull and yellow eyes, and it looked at him across the mud with the stillness of a thing deciding.

It pulled itself up the mud a coil at a time, belly scales hissing over the tussocks, head swaying that slow half-width either way, and the ground between them shrank pace by pace. The reeds whispered. Its head drew back another hand's width, the S in its neck tightening, and the strike hung in that coil like a drawn bow.

The Guild seal on it sat dull, the charm in the paper showing no READY mark — four serpents entered against the tally, the fifth line still blank. The Guild hall's lamplight followed him out into a street already settling into evening. Shop fronts were closing one by one, shutters going up with knocks that carried, and the smell of the city had shifted from dust and horse to woodsmoke and cooking fat.

"One silver two," she said, and held out her hand while the carters argued over dice behind him.

Coin crossed her palm — the silver and the two copper — and she jerked her thumb at the stairs. "Second door. Key's on the hook inside; lock it if you like. Nobody comes up but me, and I don't." She turned back to the counter, then added over her shoulder, "Bread and porridge at sixth bell if you want it. Pay in the morning for what you eat."

The room was small and honest: a real bed against the wall, a stool, the window looking down on the yard where a cart stood under sacking. He turned the key and the noise of the common room dropped to a murmur through the floorboards.

Sleep came heavy and stayed that way. The bed took the last of the marsh ache out of his shoulders somewhere in the dark hours, and the raked line on his forearm quit aching entirely; by the gray of early morning he was sleeping the flat, boneless sleep of somebody fully mended.

He woke to the yard below — a dray horse stamping, a man tossing hay down from a loft, the smell of bread rising through the window gap. Eighth bell had come and gone. Downstairs, the common room was going again: benches scraping, the girl from last night hauling a jug of something steaming along the tables, the innkeeper at the hearth with a long paddle, pulling loaves. The morning was open in front of him, and the key to the second door was still in his hand.

He was already digging out the two copper when the innkeeper turned away to the ovens — the delivery boy at the door again, second trip, and she went to box him off with a word about his mother. The coins sat in Alaric's palm with the morning heat still on them, and the counter between him and the till.

Then he was out into the street, coins back in his pouch, the morning cool and the gutters loud with wash-water. Mest's smithy announced itself two streets over by the hammer-rhythm before the sign came into view — a broad front, doors open to the yard, a boy working the bellows bar in slow strokes. Mest himself was at the anvil, sleeves rolled, a broad man gone gray at the stubble. He finished his heat, quenched it hissing, and only then looked up.

"Morning. Buy or bother?"

Alaric asked after upgrades, around four silver.

Mest wiped his hands on his apron and walked him along the rack by the wall, tapping things as he went.

"New, I'll not lie to you — four silver doesn't touch my new work. A common longsword runs ten, and that's before we talk steel worth the name." He pulled a blade down anyway, an older one, edge worn but true. "But I take trade-ins, and this came off a caravan guard who upgraded last month. Solid common work. Four silver even."

He set it down and moved along to the armor hooks.

"Armor's worse, I'll warn you now. Anything in mail or plate that's worth wearing starts past twelve, new or used." He paused at a leather jerkin, scarred at the shoulders. "This I'd let go at three silver. Soaked oil, boiled hard, took a spear-glance for its last owner and none through. Won't turn a serpent fang like your iron does, but it's lighter on the feet, if that ever matters to you."

He folded his arms and left the rack between them.

**Used Common Longsword** — 4 silver · caravan guard's trade-in, edge worn but true
**Used Leather Jerkin** — 3 silver · boiled hard, oiled, spear-scarred; light but lesser protection than his iron

"Or keep your coin," Mest said, "and come back when the serpents have paid you better. No shame in it."
